He achieved his first success at the 1993 European Youth Olympic Days and finished fourth in both the 100m and 200m freestyle at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics at age 18.

name: Geraldine Chaplin
milestone_by_age_26: Received a Golden Globe nomination for Most Promising Female Newcomer for her role as Tonya in David Lean's Doctor Zhivago (1965) at age 21, and made her Broadway debut in The Little Foxes in 1967 at age 22.
early_history_summary: Chaplin was born in Santa Monica, California, the daughter of Charlie Chaplin and Oona O'Neill, and granddaughter of playwright Eugene O'Neill. She grew up in Switzerland after her father was barred from re-entering the U.S. She studied ballet at the Royal Ballet School in London from 1961 and danced professionally in Paris before being discovered by David Lean, who cast her in Doctor Zhivago (1965).
family_context_summary: Daughter of Charlie Chaplin, one of the most famous filmmakers in history, and Oona O'Neill, daughter of Nobel Prize-winning playwright Eugene O'Neill. Grew up in Switzerland in a wealthy, culturally elite household. She herself acknowledged, 'Because of my name, the right doors opened.'
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was Charlie Chaplin, one of cinema's most iconic figures, providing direct access to the film industry. Mother was Oona O'Neill, daughter of Nobel laureate Eugene O'Neill, providing literary and cultural pedigree. The family name directly opened casting opportunities.
evidence_summary: Chaplin was born into one of cinema's most famous families as the daughter of Charlie Chaplin and granddaughter of playwright Eugene O'Neill. She grew up in Switzerland, studied ballet at the Royal Ballet School, and was discovered by director David Lean while dancing in Paris, leading to her Golden Globe-nominated debut in Doctor Zhivago (1965) at age 21. She herself acknowledged that her family name opened doors. The inherited access to the film industry, financial security, and cultural elite networks was exceptionally strong and directly catalytic to her early career.

name: Yuri Manin
milestone_by_age_26: Received his doctorate from the Steklov Mathematical Institute in 1960 at age 23 under Igor Shafarevich, was appointed Principal Researcher at Steklov, and won the Moscow Mathematical Society Award in 1963 at age 26.
early_history_summary: Manin was born in Simferopol, Crimea, and showed mathematical talent in school by improving Vinogradov's estimate of lattice points inside a sphere. He studied at Moscow State University from 1953 to 1958, where his classmates included Arnold, Kirillov, and Novikov. He published his first paper before graduating and completed his doctorate at the Steklov Institute under Shafarevich in 1960, becoming Principal Researcher there.
family_context_summary: Born in Simferopol, Crimea; father perished in World War II, mother was a teacher of literature who struggled to raise him through the war and postwar years. No evidence of family financial advantage or mathematical background.

evidence_summary: Manin was born in Simferopol to a war-widowed literature teacher and showed prodigious mathematical talent in school. He was admitted to Moscow State University, the most prestigious mathematical school in the USSR, where his classmates included Arnold, Kirillov, and Novikov. He joined Shafarevich's seminar, published his first paper before graduating, and completed his doctorate at the Steklov Institute in 1960 at age 23, becoming Principal Researcher. The elite Soviet mathematical ecosystem at MGU and Steklov, combined with Shafarevich's mentorship and a peer group of future luminaries, was the dominant early advantage. He won the Moscow Mathematical Society Award in 1963 at age 26.

name: Goran Ivanišević
milestone_by_age_26: Reached the Wimbledon singles semifinals in 1990 at age 18, the Wimbledon final in 1992 at age 20, and achieved a career-high world ranking of No. 2 in July 1994 at age 22, all well before age 26.
early_history_summary: Ivanišević was born in Split, Croatia (then Yugoslavia), to an engineering professor father and chemical engineer mother. He began tennis at age seven, was trained by Jelena Genčić, and turned professional in 1988 at age 17. His parents sold their house to fund his private coaching. He made the Australian Open quarterfinals as a qualifier in 1989 at age 17, reached the Wimbledon semifinals in 1990 at age 18, and the Wimbledon final in 1992 at age 20.
family_context_summary: Born in Split, Yugoslavia, to Srđan Ivanišević, an engineering professor who also played tennis, and Gorana, a chemical engineer. His parents sold their house to fund his private tennis coaching, demonstrating significant family financial sacrifice and commitment to his career.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an engineering professor who played tennis recreationally, introducing Goran to the sport at age seven. Parents made extraordinary financial sacrifice by selling their house to fund coaching. Key mentor was Jelena Genčić, who trained him as a boy.
evidence_summary: Ivanišević was born in Split to an engineering professor father who introduced him to tennis at age seven. His parents sold their house to fund private coaching, and he was trained by Jelena Genčić, a key mentor. He turned professional at 17 in 1988, made the Australian Open quarterfinals as a qualifier in 1989 at age 17, and reached the Wimbledon semifinals in 1990 at age 18. By age 20 he reached the Wimbledon final and won Olympic bronze. His lethal left-handed serve was his signature shot from age 12. The combination of early specialization, family financial sacrifice, dedicated mentoring, and prodigious physical talent drove his early breakthrough.
